All the impressions that I feel at this moment come from physical nature, from the world of manifested forms. # On the Revolution of the
## Late Winter, and what occurs
## therein.

<note>A decorative initial letter W.</note>
We wish to have the entire year divided into five
parts, namely:
Late Winter, Spring <note>original: "Lenz"</note>, Summer,
Autumn, and Early Winter. We shall briefly
treat three things concerning these: the arrangement <term>Disposition</term> <gloss>astrological positioning</gloss> of the heavens and their influence <term>Influentz</term> <gloss>the flowing power of the stars</gloss>, the eclipses and their significance, and then
the changes in the air <note>weather patterns</note>.

Firstly, concerning the Late Winter,
which follows immediately after the old year,
and extends from Saint Lucia's Day 1595 until Saint Gregory's Day 1596. It begins
in the preceding civil year of 1595, on the 12th day
of December <note>original: "Christmonats"</note>, in the afternoon at 4 o'clock and 40
minutes. At that time, a few days prior, the Sun <term>Sol</term> <gloss>the Sun</gloss> and Venus
set with the star Arcturus, which caused wind. Around that time, in the geographic height of the land of Basel, the 10th degree of Cancer <term>Cancri</term> <gloss>the Crab</gloss> shows itself in the morning corner. At the peak of the heavens is found the 7th degree of Pisces <note>original: "Fisch"</note>, in which
25th degree Jupiter then had its course,
and makes itself heard as a ruler on account of an exceeding prerogative <note>original: "propter nimiam prærogativam"</note>.

# Physics, Book III

<margin>

...upon the mover, so that to move is to exercise this activity upon the movable. <margin>note this</margin>
**A**nd for this reason, motion is the fulfillment <note>original: "entelecheia"; often translated as "actuality," it refers to the state of a thing having reached its full potential or functional end.</note> of the movable, insofar as it is movable. This happens through contact with the mover, so that the mover also undergoes an effect at the same time. The mover will always bring some form <note>original: "eidos"; the defining characteristic or "blueprint" of a thing.</note>, whether it be substance, quality, or quantity, which will be the principle and cause of the motion when it moves; for example, a man who is actually a man produces a man from what is potentially a man. And the puzzle is also clear: that motion is in the moved. For it is the fulfillment brought about by the mover itself. And the activity <note>original: "energeia"; the state of being "at work" or in operation.</note> of the mover is not something else; for there must be a fulfillment of both. For a thing is "capable of moving" by its potential, but it "moves" by its activity; yet it is active upon the moved, so that the activity of both is similarly one, just as the interval of one to two is the same as two to one, and the uphill is the same as the downhill. For these are one thing, though their definition <note>original: "logos"; here meaning the rational account or formula that explains what a thing is.</note> is not one. So it is also with the mover and the moved. <margin>the motion is in the thing being moved</margin>
This poses a logical puzzle: for it is necessary that there be some distinct activity for each. One is "acting" <note>original: "poiesis"; the process of making or doing.</note> and the other is "undergoing" <note>original: "pathesis"; the process of being acted upon or receiving an impression.</note>; the work and the end of the former is a "product," and of the latter an "affection." Since both are motions, if they are different, in what do they reside? For either both are in the one being acted upon and moved, or the acting is in the actor and the undergoing is in the sufferer (but if we must call this latter one "acting" as well, the term would be used equivocally). But if the acting is in the actor, motion will be in the mover—for the same reasoning applies to both mover and moved. Thus, either everything that moves will itself be moved, or it will possess motion without being moved. But if both are in the moved and the sufferer—both the acting and the undergoing—and teaching and learning, being two, are both in the learner, then first, the activity of each will not exist in each, and second, it is absurd for two motions to be moved at once. For what are these two alterations of the one thing toward one form? That is impossible.

<column-break/>

### Page 3

<margin>
<unclear>... it is not absurd for the activity of one to be in another ...</unclear>
</margin>

...but the activity will be one. Yet it is irrational for the activity of two things that differ in kind to be one and the same; and it will be so if teaching and learning are the same, as are acting and undergoing—to teach would be the same as to learn, and to act the same as to undergo, so that the teacher would necessarily have to learn everything, and the actor to suffer. Or is it neither absurd that the activity of one should be in another (for teaching is the activity of the person capable of teaching, yet it is *in* something, not cut off, but the activity *of* this person *in* that person); nor does anything prevent one activity from being the same for two, not in the sense that their "being" <note>original: "to einai"; the essential existence or essence of the thing.</note> is the same, but in the way the potential stands toward the active.
**T**he activity, as the genus of the underlying subject, is the same; like the interval from one to two and from two to one, or the uphill and the downhill road. For these are one, though the definition is not one. The same applies to the mover and the moved. How then is it not necessary for the teacher to learn, if acting and undergoing are the same? They are not the same in the sense that their definition of "what it is to be" <note>original: "to ti en einai"; Aristotle’s technical phrase for "essence."</note> is one, like "garment" and "cloak," but like the road from Thebes to Athens and the road from Athens to Thebes, as was said before. For not all the same things belong to everything that is in some way "the same," but only to those whose essence is the same. Moreover, even if teaching is the same as learning, "to learn" is not the same as "to teach"; just as, even if there is one distance between two separate things, "to be distant from here to there" is not one and the same as "to be distant from there to here." In general, neither teaching and learning nor acting and undergoing are the same in the strict sense, but that to which these belong—the motion—is the same. For to be the activity of *this* in *that*, and the activity of *that* by *this*, are different in definition.
We have now said what motion is, both generally and specifically. For it is not unclear how each of its types will be defined; for alteration <note>original: "alloiosis"; qualitative change.</note> is the fulfillment of the alterable, insofar as it is alterable. Still more clearly, it is the fulfillment of the potential to act and to be acted upon, insofar as they are such, both generally and again specifically, whether it be house-building or healing. Each of the other motions will be spoken of in the same way.

### CAPVT. I.
### Segregationis aquarum apparatus.

<margin>A</margin> QVA ipsa vel tota in se consideratur, vel in compositionis membra segregata, quorum deinceps vnum quodque pro se spectatur. Vtrobique communia sunt multa. Vt itaque per segregationes perueniamus ad notitiam partium compositionis: Est enim omnis aqua mineralis ex genere imperfecte mistorum: haurienda ab ipso fonte est certa quantitas, quo tempore maximè est sui, valet virtute, liberaque est a turbis elementaribus, ab iniuria animalium, áque similibus externis; quod fieri posse iudicant tempore sereno diutius, ante autumnum paulo, sub auroram, cum quieuerit satis ab haurientibus, potantibusue, cum venti non bacchantur &c. estque instituenda segregatio non procul a fonte, ne dum longius effertur spirituum quorumdam iacturam capiat. Vasa sint vitrea, aut lapidea, impenetrabilia halitibus, aut succis mordacibus, nisi cum examinis ratio requirit aut permittit etiam metallica, lignea, figulina fara, &c.

### CAP. II.
### Segregatio spirituum.

<margin>A</margin> Quae pondus certum statim mittatur in cucurbitam cum alembico, cuius rostrum transeat per refrigeria, aut ipse instratus sit refrigeratoriis pannis, &c. Apponatur excipulus, tenaciq; maltha commissurae omnes obstruantur quam exactissimè. Cucurbita in fimo leni, vel balneo vaporis, aut saltem maris tepido locetur, vt abstrahantur spiritus subtilissimi. Hi examinentur sigillatim, sicut & aqua in cucurbita relicta. Postea comparentur, vt constet in quanam parte virtus sit potior. Potest & vtraque ad pondus reuocari. ### CAP. III.

<margin>S</margin> Ed siue aliquid prodierit, siue nihil, transferatur vas in cineres, & prouocetur pars aquosa vsque ad consistentiam melleam, si talis fore iudicabitur. Partes spectentur item seorsim, & postea inter se conferantur. Quod residuum est, perfundatur aliqua parte extractae aquae (si quidem iudicabitur aliqua crassa consistentia) & immaceretur. Si ne tunc quidem hypostasis inuenitur, destilletur, vel diuaporatur prorsus. Vbi enim nulla fit secessio, nec inueniuntur reliquae, spiritalis tota est contemperatio, aestimabiturque virtus, & natura ex destillato & residuo per collationem mutuam. On the Judgment of Mineral Waters, Part 2.

# A TREATISE ON MINERAL WATERS
## PART TWO.

### CHAPTER I.
### The apparatus for the separation of waters.

<margin>A</margin> Water itself is considered either as a whole in itself, or as separated into its component parts, each of which is then viewed on its own. In both cases, many things are held in common. We will first examine those things which are closer to the senses; then those which belong more to reason, that is, the effects: before which we will place the methods of separation that are usually adapted to this matter.

So that we may arrive at a knowledge of the component parts through separation—for every mineral water is of the category of "imperfect mixtures"—a certain quantity must be drawn from the spring itself at the time when it is most truly itself, strong in its power, and free from elemental disturbances, from the harm caused by animals, and from similar external factors. This is judged to be possible during a long period of clear weather, shortly before autumn, at dawn, when the spring has rested enough from those drawing or drinking it, and when the winds are not raging, etc. The separation should be established not far from the spring, lest it suffer a loss of certain spirits <term>spirituum<gloss>volatile components or essences</gloss></term> while being carried further away. The vessels should be of glass or stone, impenetrable to vapors or corrosive juices, unless the nature of the examination requires or even permits metallic, wooden, or earthenware <term>figulina fara<gloss>pottery vessels</gloss></term> ones, etc.

### CHAPTER II.
### The separation of spirits.

<margin>A</margin> Once a certain weight has been measured, let it be immediately put into a cucurbit <term>cucurbitam<gloss>a gourd-shaped glass vessel used in distillation</gloss></term> with an alembic <term>alembico<gloss>the cap or head of a still</gloss></term>, whose beak should pass through cooling systems, or let it be covered with cooling cloths, etc. Let a receiver <term>excipulus<gloss>a vessel to catch the distillate</gloss></term> be attached, and let all the joints be blocked as precisely as possible with tenacious mastic <term>maltha<gloss>a cement or putty used to seal laboratory equipment</gloss></term>. Let the cucurbit be placed in gentle dung <note>Dung was used as a source of low, steady heat for "digesting" substances.</note>, or a vapor bath, or at least a lukewarm water bath <term>balneo maris<gloss>literally a "bath of the sea"; a bain-marie</gloss></term>, so that the most subtle spirits may be drawn off. Let these be examined one by one, as well as the water left in the cucurbit. Afterward, let them be compared, so that it may be clear in which part the power is more potent. Both can also be reduced to their weight. But if none or very few are drawn out, it must be judged that the mixture is rather "corpulent" <note>Thick or heavy</note>, or, if you prefer, that the spirits are more earthy, like juices dissolved in the liquid.

### CHAPTER III.
### Separation of the wateriness and the contents.

<margin>S</margin> But whether something has come forth or nothing, let the vessel be transferred to the ashes <note>A sand or ash bath allows for higher heat than a water bath.</note>, and let the watery part be provoked until it reaches a honey-like consistency, if such is judged to be appropriate. Let the parts be viewed separately likewise, and then compared with one another. What remains should be drenched with some part of the extracted water (if indeed a certain thick consistency is judged) and allowed to soak. Afterward, let it be poured off. Let the poured-off liquid be coagulated to the thickness of lye, alum, and similar juices. Then let either straws, or small cords, or little rods, etc., be placed into both parts. And let coagulation be expected, or else let evaporation <term>diuaporatio<gloss>slow evaporation by heat</gloss></term> occur in a glass shell gradually by the heat of the furnace in a closed vessel. The contents will be at the bottom. If no thickness appears after the greater part of the subtle matter has been exhausted, let it be set to "putrefy" <note>In early chemistry, this refers to a slow digestion or fermentation process, not necessarily rotting.</note> for a month. If even then no sediment <term>hypostasis<gloss>a deposit or sediment</gloss></term> is found, let it be distilled or evaporated entirely. For where no separation occurs and no remains are found, the entire mixture is of a spiritual nature, and its power and nature will be estimated from the distillate and the residue through mutual comparison. Note, however, that where you have separated the thinnest spirits by the gentlest heat, in the second distillation over ashes, with the receiver changed and kept movable during the distillation, the drops should be observed and tasted more frequently. For if they taste of the same mineral power, or exhibit a new one, or are even tasteless like water, you will be able to determine the method of separation more exactly, and receive different liquids in different vessels. It is also possible to note by sight when the invisible spirits cease and are succeeded by watery ones. For then the alembic "sweats" and is marked by little streams. By this method alone, if you act skillfully, you will be able to draw out the most essential parts. For the first operation provides the spirits; the second, the heavier waters, whether mineral or tasteless and pure. The third separates the solidifiable juices from the "limes" <term>calcibus<gloss>residues left after calcination or evaporation</gloss></term>, and indeed alum from vitriol <term>attramento<gloss>literally "ink," often used for vitriol or copperas</gloss></term>, salt from niter <term>halinitro<gloss>a natural saltpeter or soda</gloss></term>, etc.
